sentences.text: A black woodpecker makes a nest hole about eight metres up and shaped like a keyhole, and there are forty or fifty of them in the Bjurholm forest and Nils could show you every one.
The doors are different.
They are at eye height — his eye height, and his father's, and his grandmother's, which is a range of about thirty centimetres and which is the first thing about them that does not make sense.
Nils measured all nine at fourteen, with a tape, because he had got tired of people saying *about eye height* as though that meant anything.
The lowest is a hundred and forty-one centimetres and the highest is a hundred and seventy-two.
His grandmother's eye, at the time, was a hundred and forty-eight.
His own is a hundred and seventy-nine and he has to stoop for every single one of them, which he did not expect and which annoyed him for about a year.
They are round and they are the width of a fist and they go straight in, and there are nine of them in about four hundred hectares.
They are always in a living tree.
Never a snag, never a stump, never anything rotten.
Four of the nine are in spruce, which no woodpecker in Sweden would bother with, and one is in a birch that Nils's father says has been there since the war.
That is the part a forester notices first.
Woodpeckers go for dead and dying wood because dead wood is soft and full of what they eat, and a healthy spruce is the last thing on the list — hard, resinous, and empty.
There is also no woodpecker in that forest that makes a round hole a fist wide at a metre and a half.
The great spotted makes a smaller one higher up.
The black makes a bigger one, oval, at eight metres.
Nils has looked this up in three books and has never found a species that would account for a single one of the nine.
And you can look in.
That is the whole of it and it is not much to say out loud.
You put your eye to a hole in a tree and you look, and you see the inside of the tree.
Not a hollow.
There is no hollow; if you put a stick in, the stick goes in about four centimetres and stops on solid wood, and Nils has done this and can confirm it and has felt extremely stupid doing it.

What you see, with your eye against the bark, is the wood from inside — the whole cylinder of it, going away from you in both directions, and every ring lit from somewhere and stacked outward from the middle in the order they were made.
It is lit.
He does not know from where and neither did his grandmother and there is no light source anywhere in a tree.
What there is is enough of it to see by, evenly, with no shadows and no direction, in the way that a page in a book is lit when you are not thinking about the lamp.
You are looking at the years.
